source_text: So here's an interesting thing about active inference, which is, I've started to report on the amount of time it takes per click and the amount of tokens that are used a recent one, It was like a million tokens I don't know if that's a lot or a little for the work that was done, because, you know, we're not just doing the work that comes after selecting and thinking about which I had to do we're doing all that work leading up to the selection, and then doing the selection, and then thinking about what to do oh, that might be a lot, but we should keep track of how much, and I think ultimately it would be good to try to make those things efficient as well so we've got, you know, lots of different hoops and rulings that this thing has got to jump through but I think this is another one I would say it perhaps could be part of R20 as an additional criterion, Anyway, Codex 10 had developed a repeatable way to evaluate the behavior of the machine, but that was kind of a generic evaluation, not necessarily an evaluation that included this R20 certificate so I think we should ten that it can run another click and that we would like to evaluate the results.

reply_text:
㊥ ("it can run another click") I will pass that to codex-10 as soon as its current job returns: one more click, evaluated with its own procedure plus the R20 certificate and the click's time and token cost. The click goes after the census rewrite on purpose, so that the run it produces carries the new certificate.

㊟ (why not this minute) codex-10 is mid-job on the census rewrite. Two reasons to wait for it:
- A click run now would end with the old census, which reports on evidence nothing writes.
- If I then fixed review findings in the census while that click was in the air, the runner would refuse the click for stale source.

So the order is: census returns, I review and fix, then the click.

㊢ ("keep track of how much") The run record already carries what a cost row needs. I read the producer:
- **Tokens:** `:registered-run/model-usage` lists every job the click dispatched, with its role, phase and input, output and cached counts. It also says whether the accounting is complete, partial or missing.
- **Time:** `:registered-run/timing` has per-phase times, with selection broken into sub-phases since yesterday's commits.

So the split you describe ("all that work leading up to the selection, and then doing the selection") can be read off per click without new instrumentation.

㊭ ("part of R20 as an additional criterion") A ninth row, cost.
- **Prints:** tokens and time before selection, at selection and after it, and which side the click spent most on.
- **Agrees when:** the accounting is complete, meaning every dispatched job has a usage record and the parts add up to the total.
- **No threshold yet:** I would not set a pass mark for "too many tokens". There is no basis for one until several clicks have been measured, so I can't say whether a million is a lot.

㊟ (what the theory offers for efficiency) Parr et al. (§10.8) treat this as bounded rationality: an agent "has to balance the costs, effort, and timeliness of computation", and "what is costly during deliberation is decreasing the entropy ... of one's beliefs before a choice". That suggests comparing what deliberation spent with how much it sharpened the choice among policies. A figure such as "nats gained per million tokens" would be my construction from that passage, not something the book defines. I would report it alongside the raw numbers first and only later consider it as a criterion.

㊯ (the click job for codex-10, queued behind the census) The packet will carry:
- your words as the grant for one more click, since codex-10 records grants in the click-budget file;
- its existing repeatable evaluation, unchanged;
- the R20 certificate from the run record, row by row;
- tokens and time by phase from the two records above.

The cost row itself (Lean and census) follows as a separate small job, so the click is not held up by it.

- **Park:** `park-9bc43b93-6253-4bcc-8dda-db61123af70c`.
- **Memory:** your cost direction is saved with the R20 note.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-2

previous_reply_acts.text:
(what R20 adds) Two things the earlier proofs did not have:
- **The case in plain words:** each row names which case of the theory held, as in your "F is the same for every policy" example.
- **One verdict for the click:** certified when every row agrees with its record. A missing record makes the row say "not recorded", and the click is then not certified.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-2
previous_reply_acts.text:
(precision, reviewed) codex-10's restatement at the fixed point is accepted (mathlib4 `983ba69d4d`), with my fixes in `dacfbe3506`. What I checked and changed:
- **Record:** no `sorry`, `axiom` or `native_decide`; the three build logs pass and are committed.
- **Definitions:** the habit term is in both distributions, and the error term is Friston's.
- **First control:** it covered one of four cases and was not about the record. It now says a record whose temperature did not move under any discriminating observation does not conform.
- **Second control:** it assumed the inequality it was named for. I proved it.
- **Unused hypothesis:** the direction theorems never needed the habit to be positive, so I removed that hypothesis.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-2
previous_reply_acts.text: (precision, limit) The existence of a settling temperature is not proved in general. codex-10 declined to claim it, which is the right call; a proof needs the behaviour of the error near zero temperature. It is proved to be unique when the observation does not discriminate.

previous_reply_acts.text:
(R20 job, running) The module imports the eight node modules and adds no new theory.
- **Rows:** precision, evidence, habit, class preference, strategic focus, liveness, author-is-not-reviewer, and the two-agent joint action.
- **Proved:** the click is certified exactly when every node has a record that conforms, and each node's existing control record yields a "disagrees" row.
